guide.summary: This unit covers magnetic forces on moving charges and currents, motion of charges in magnetic fields, torque on current loops, and calculating magnetic fields with the Biot–Savart law and Ampère's law for wires, loops, solenoids, toroids, and thick conductors.

sections.heading: Magnetic forces
sections.body: Force on a moving charge: F = qv × B, perpendicular to both v and B, so it does no work. A charge moving perpendicular to uniform B moves in a circle: r = mv/(|q|B), with period T = 2πm/(|q|B) independent of speed (cyclotron frequency). Velocity components parallel to B are unaffected, producing helical paths. Force on a current-carrying wire: F = ∫I dℓ × B; for a straight wire in uniform field, F = IℓB sin θ. Parallel currents attract with force per length μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd). A current loop has magnetic dipole moment μ = NIA (direction by right-hand rule) and experiences torque τ = μ × B, which tends to align μ with B; its potential energy is U = −μ·B.

sections.heading: Biot–Savart law
sections.body: dB = (μ₀/4π) I dℓ × r̂/r². Integrate over the current, using symmetry. Results: center of a circular loop, B = μ₀I/(2R); center of an arc subtending angle φ, B = μ₀Iφ/(4πR) (semicircle: μ₀I/(4R)); on the axis of a loop, B = μ₀IR²/[2(R² + x²)^(3/2)]; infinite straight wire, B = μ₀I/(2πr); straight segments contribute nothing at points along their own line.

sections.heading: Ampère's law
sections.body: ∮B·dℓ = μ₀I_enc around any closed loop; useful for calculating B with high symmetry. Long straight wire: B = μ₀I/(2πr). Inside a thick wire of radius R with uniform current density: B = μ₀Ir/(2πR²) (∝ r). Ideal solenoid: B = μ₀nI inside (n = turns per length), uniform, and approximately zero outside. Toroid: B = μ₀NI/(2πr) inside, zero outside. Coaxial cable with equal and opposite currents: B = 0 outside.

sections.heading: Worked example: force on a moving charge
sections.body: A proton moving at 2.0 × 10⁶ m/s enters a uniform 0.10 T magnetic field perpendicular to its velocity. The magnetic force qvB provides centripetal force, so the radius of its circular path is r = mv/(qB) = (1.67 × 10⁻²⁷)(2.0 × 10⁶)/((1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)(0.10)) ≈ 0.21 m. The magnetic force does no work because it is always perpendicular to velocity, so the proton's speed stays constant. Use the right-hand rule for positive charges and reverse the direction for negative charges.

sections.heading: Worked example: Ampère's law
sections.body: For a long straight wire carrying current I, choose a circular Amperian loop of radius r centered on the wire. By symmetry, B is constant and tangent to the loop, so B(2πr) = μ₀I and B = μ₀I/(2πr). Inside a long solenoid with n turns per meter, a rectangular loop gives B = μ₀nI, uniform inside and nearly zero outside. Ampère's law works when symmetry makes B constant along the path; otherwise, use the Biot–Savart law, as for the field at the center of a circular loop, B = μ₀I/(2R).

sections.heading: Forces between currents
sections.body: Parallel wires carrying current in the same direction attract, and wires carrying current in opposite directions repel. The force per unit length is μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd). A current loop in a magnetic field experiences a torque τ = μ × B, where μ = NIA, which is the principle behind electric motors.

sections.heading: Going deeper
sections.body: The Biot–Savart law, dB = (μ₀/4π)(I dl × r̂)/r², finds fields from arbitrary current shapes. For a circular loop of radius R at a point on its axis a distance x from the center, B = μ₀IR²/(2(R² + x²)^(3/2)), which reduces to μ₀I/(2R) at the center. Free-response questions may ask you to set up the integral, use symmetry to cancel components, and evaluate it.

sections.heading: Key terms
sections.body: Know magnetic force, the right-hand rule, cyclotron radius, Biot–Savart law, Ampère's law, solenoid, magnetic dipole moment, and torque on a current loop. A charged particle moving parallel to a magnetic field feels no magnetic force, while one moving at an angle follows a helical path. The velocity selector uses crossed electric and magnetic fields so that only particles with v = E/B pass undeflected.

keyTakeaways: F = qv × B; no work done.
r = mv/qB; period independent of speed.
Loop center: μ₀I/2R; long wire: μ₀I/2πr.
Torque on loop: τ = μ × B, μ = NIA.
commonMistakes: Using Ampère's law where symmetry doesn't make B constant along the loop.
Forgetting the vector cross product direction (and the sign for negative charges).
Using total current instead of enclosed current inside a thick wire.
Thinking the magnetic force changes a particle's speed.
Including contributions from straight segments collinear with the field point.
examTips: Biot–Savart setups: write dℓ, r̂, and the angle explicitly before integrating.
B(r) graphs for thick wires: linear inside, 1/r outside, continuous at R.
Superpose fields from multiple wires as vectors.
For a loop in a field, state the torque direction and the equilibrium orientation.

vocab.definition: T = 2πm/(qB), the period of circular motion in a uniform magnetic field.
μ = NIA for a current loop, directed by the right-hand rule.
dB = (μ₀/4π) I dℓ × r̂/r², the field from a current element.
A closed path chosen to exploit symmetry with Ampère's law.

practice.stem: A circular loop of radius 0.10 m carries 5.0 A. What is the magnetic field at its center? (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A)
A long solenoid has 1,000 turns per meter and carries 2.0 A. What is the field inside?
A proton moves in a circle perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field. If its speed doubles, its period of revolution
practice.explanation: T = 2πm/(qB); radius doubles but so does speed.

practice.stem: Two long parallel wires 5.0 cm apart each carry 10 A in the same direction. What is the force per unit length between them?
practice.explanation: F/ℓ = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd) = (2 × 10⁻⁷)(100)/0.050 = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ N/m; same-direction currents attract.

practice.stem: A long solid cylindrical wire of radius R carries current I uniformly distributed over its cross-section. What is B at r = R/2?

distractors.B: Uses total current at r = R/2.

practice.stem: A 50-turn rectangular coil of area 0.010 m² carries 2.0 A in a 0.50 T field. What is the maximum torque on it?

A wire carrying current I consists of a semicircle of radius R connected to two long straight leads that lie along lines passing through the semicircle's center. What is the magnetic field at the center?
practice.explanation: Radial leads contribute nothing (dℓ ∥ r̂). The semicircle gives half of a full loop's μ₀I/2R.

practice.stem: An electron enters a uniform magnetic field with velocity at 30° to the field direction. Its path is

choices.text: a helix around the field direction

practice.explanation: The parallel component is unchanged while the perpendicular component produces circular motion.

practice.stem: A coaxial cable has current I in the inner conductor and current I in the opposite direction in the outer conductor. What is the magnetic field outside the cable?
practice.explanation: An Amperian loop outside encloses zero net current.

practice.stem: A current loop is free to rotate in a uniform magnetic field. In which orientation is it in stable equilibrium?

choices.text: Its plane is parallel to B.
Its magnetic moment is antiparallel to B.
Its magnetic moment is parallel to B.

practice.explanation: U = −μ·B is minimum when μ ∥ B.

practice.stem: What is the magnetic field on the axis of a circular loop (radius R, current I) at distance x from its center, for x ≫ R?
practice.explanation: B = μ₀IR²/[2(R² + x²)^(3/2)] → μ₀IR²/(2x³), a dipole field ∝ 1/x³.

practice.stem: A long hollow conducting cylinder with inner radius a and outer radius b carries current I uniformly through its cross-section. What is B at radius r with a < r < b?
practice.explanation: I_enc = I(r² − a²)/(b² − a²); B(2πr) = μ₀I_enc.

practice.stem: A rigid wire shaped as a semicircle of radius R lies in a plane perpendicular to a uniform field B, with its ends on a straight line, and carries current I. What is the magnitude of the net magnetic force on the semicircle?
practice.explanation: In a uniform field, the net force on any wire equals that on a straight wire joining its ends (length 2R).

distractors.B: Uses arc length without vector cancellation.

practice.stem: A toroid has N turns, inner radius a, and outer radius b, carrying current I. How does the field inside its core vary with r?
practice.explanation: A circular Amperian loop of radius r inside encloses NI.

practice.prompt: A long, straight, solid cylindrical wire of radius R carries a current I uniformly distributed across its cross-section.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: A student claims the magnetic field is greatest at the center of the wire because that is where the current is 'most concentrated.' Without equations, explain whether the field is greatest at the center, at the surface, or far outside.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Using Ampère's law, derive expressions for B inside (r < R) and outside (r > R) the wire.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Explain how your expressions support or contradict your reasoning in (A).

rubric.description: The field is greatest at the surface; it is zero at the center.
At the center, contributions from current on all sides cancel by symmetry (no current enclosed); moving outward, more current is enclosed.
Outside, enclosed current is fixed while the distance grows, so the field weakens.
I_enc = I r²/R²; B(2πr) = μ₀I r²/R² → B = μ₀Ir/(2πR²).
States circular Amperian loop with B tangent and constant by symmetry.
Inside B ∝ r (zero at center, increasing); outside B ∝ 1/r (decreasing).
Both give μ₀I/(2πR) at r = R, the maximum, supporting (A) and contradicting the student.

practice.sampleResponse:
A. The field is greatest at the surface, not the center. At the center, current flows symmetrically on all sides, and the contributions cancel; an Amperian loop of zero radius encloses no current. Moving outward, a loop encloses more and more current, so the field grows. Outside the wire, the loop always encloses the full current, but the loop's circumference grows with r, so the field decreases. The maximum occurs at the surface.

B. By symmetry, B is tangent to circles centered on the wire and has constant magnitude on each. Ampère's law: B(2πr) = μ₀I_enc.
Inside: I_enc = I(πr²/πR²) = Ir²/R², so B = μ₀Ir/(2πR²).
Outside: I_enc = I, so B = μ₀I/(2πr).

C. Inside, B is proportional to r, starting at zero at the center and increasing; outside, B is proportional to 1/r, decreasing. Both expressions equal μ₀I/(2πR) at r = R, so the field peaks at the surface. This supports my reasoning in (A) and contradicts the student's claim.
